Thank you for your positive feedback. We deeply appreciate your acknowledgment and the helpful comments you have given.

**Q1: The paper could strengthen its contribution by including a comparison of ChessGPT and ChessCLIP to state-of-the-art (SOTA) chess models in the appendix. This would provide a better context for evaluating the effectiveness of the proposed models and approach. At the moment it is hard to put these models ability in perspective. It is unlikely these models outperform powerful methods like AlphaZero but it would be helpful to evaluate how close you can get to these other methods with this language model approach.**

A1: Thank you for the feedback. It’s essential to note that the primary objective of ChessGPT and ChessCLIP is to delve into the relationship between policy learning and language modeling, rather than purely achieving top-tier chess performance. While models like Leela Chess Zero[1], AlphaZero[2], and Stockfish[3] are tailored for chess with intricate search strategies, our models emphasize the integration of game data with natural language insights. Direct comparisons might not capture the distinct goals of each approach. However, we recognize the value of such evaluations and are considering them for future work. Our aim is to shed light on the potential of merging language modeling with game playing, even if it doesn’t match the raw skill of dedicated chess AIs.


**Q2: it is unsurprising that these models outperform general LLMs that are not fine tuned for this task. In fact, these baseline LLMs do relatively poorly on most of these evaluations. Since there isn't a clear previous finetuned LLM baseline to compare against that I know of, it may be more fruitful for the authors to evaluate what the most valuable information sources in their dataset are for valuation performance.**

A2: Thank you for your comment. We agree with your point that it will be more fruitful to identify the most valuable information in our database. However, due to the large computing resources required to conduct the base training, we are still working on it and will add more analysis in our future version. Currently, based on our experimental results, we believe the annotated game dataset is the most valuable information in our dataset. A piece of direct evidence is that ChessCLIP was only trained on the annotated dataset but can show comparable or even better performance on several value judgement evaluation tasks.

To illustrate, an example from this dataset is an annotated PGN with the Sicilian Defense opening:

1.e4 c5 {The game starts with the Sicilian Defense, one of the most popular and aggressive responses to 1.e4. Black aims to control the center and create imbalances early on.}

These annotations provide rich insights into the thought process, strategic considerations, and tactical ideas behind each move, bridging the gap between board state and human language.

**Q3: As a non-chess expert, it was hard for me to completely understand the detail of their evaluations. Some visualizations might be helpful here.**

A3: Thank you for your feedback. Recognizing the complexity of the datasets, especially for non-chess experts, we have incorporated additional figures and illustrative examples to enhance the paper’s clarity and presentation, including the figure 1, dataset examples and evaluation task examples (see our global response for details). We believe these new visualizations will provide a more intuitive understanding of our work.

**Q4: The models, as currently presented, do not appear to have the ability to learn from their own gameplay experiences in contrast to RL algorithms, which is a limitation for the further enhancement of their policies. While this limitation could potentially be addressed in future work, the current models might not fully capture the dynamic nature of decision-making processes in the context of games.**

A4: Thank you for highlighting this limitation. Our models, as they stand, don’t learn from gameplay like RL algorithms. However, our focus is on the synergy between policy learning and language modeling in chess. We leverage annotated game data and language insights, offering a unique angle grounded in human expertise.

Moreover, one of our main contributions is the benchmark we’ve introduced. The model we presented is an initial attempt, and we encourage further research in this area. We hope our benchmark spurs interest and guides the community in exploring dynamic decision-making in games, as you suggested.

Reference:

[1] Pascutto G.C., Linscott G., Lyashuk A., Huizinga F. Leela Chess Zero. Available online: https://lczero.org

[2] Silver, David, et al. “A general reinforcement learning algorithm that masters chess, shogi, and Go through self-play.” Science 362.6419 (2018): 1140-1144.

[3] Romstad T., Costalba M., Kiiski J., Linscott G., Nicolet S., Geschwentner S., VandeVondele J. Stockfish. Version 14. Available online: https://stockfishchess.org

**Q1: Post data collection and synthesis, it is necessary to analyze data quality of the collection e.g. vocabulary, sentence similarity etc. you can find more such parameters in the literature such as https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.746.pdf, and https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00816. My hypothesis is, not every dataset in the collection add to the inductive bias, there might be some negative interference across datasets which could be an interesting avenue to study. This study could improve model performance further.**

A1:Thank you for your constructive comment. We have included a new section in Appendix D to offer more data analysis results including dataset statistics, examples and some metrics which we hope would be helpful in understanding the quality of the dataset. 
We are still investigating utilizing [1] and [2] to further analyze our dataset. This was more difficult than we anticipated as [1] requires retraining our models which we are unable to do at the moment and we found that the approach taken [2] may not be computationally fast enough for us to apply at our scale.

We do note that some of the analysis used for typical NLP corpus may not be as informative in our case as we found anecdotally that examples that contain chess terminology and notation have a tendency to be considered “unnatural” and filtered by pipelines that was designed for natural language corpus. This is especially pronounced for PGNs which are distinctively different from the language dataset.
[1] https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.746.pdf
[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00816

**Q2: Doing a detailed human error analysis can help get more insights about these type of findings.**

A2: Thank you for your constructive comment. In accordance with your suggestion, we have added new human error analysis in our qualitative analysis in Appendix H. 

**Q3: Post collecting instruction-tuning data from GPT4, authors might want to experiment with different instruction/prompt formats since models are sensitive to this e.g. see https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02707 and https://aclanthology.org/2022.findings-acl.50.pdf**

A3: Thank you for your insights. We concur that GPT-4 exhibits considerable sensitivity to seed prompts used during data collection. Nevertheless, within our dataset, which encompasses numerous data subsets, the portion acquired from GPT-4 is relatively minor, playing a relatively less pivotal role in the training of our chat model. Please refer to Table 9 in Appendix D.1 for a detailed breakdown of data statistics. We leave such investigation for future work.

**Q4: Authors may want to revisit some of the phrasings in this paper e.g. L72 "collecting all chess-related materials from the Internet", L70 "care more".**

A4: Thanks for pointing out the mistakes. We have rephrased our sentences to make them more appropriate (in line 74 and 77).

**Q5: Yes. I would suggest authors to add relevant instruction tuning literature, since their method is based on instruction tuning. For example: https://aclanthology.org/2022.acl-long.244.pdf, https://openreview.net/forum?id=gEZrGCozdqR**

In addition, we also thoroughly include illustrations of the significance and core insights for each subset. For instance, we include the collection consideration of the ELO rating of the game dataset, which is why we choose different sources of the game dataset.

**Q3: The author's literature review appears to be lacking, as the references cited seem insufficient and inaccurate. In line 22, the author references three papers in the context of models leveraging Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). ....**

A3: Thank you for your comment. The full sentence in our original paper is ‘models leveraging Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback’. We want to clarify here that our references are in fact references to the word ‘models’, which means that these models utilized the technique of RLHF, instead of the word ‘RLHF’. To alleviate such confusion, we have modified the sentence in L22 and 23 for clearer references.

**Q4: How does the author perceive the significance of the following two papers in the context of RLHF?
Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences, Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback**

A4: Thank you for pointing out the missing literature. We have added the first literature in L23 about RLHF.

**Q5: After reading the entire paper, it seems that the author summarized relevant online chess data to train ChessGPT, a 2.8B parameter pre-trained language model (mentioned in the hugging face dataset description as Model Description: A 2.8B parameter pre-trained language model in Chess.). ...**

A5: In fact, 3B is a rounded representation of 2.8B and this is a commonly adopted naming method in many different LLMs, such as Redpajama-3B (which is in fact 2.8B, refer to https://huggingface.co/togethercomputer/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1#model-details) and ChatGLM-6B (which is in fact 6.2B, refer to https://github.com/THUDM/ChatGLM-6B/blob/main/README_en.md#introduction). To alleviate such confusion, we add a footnote for clarification in L251.

**Q6: In line 41, it is mentioned, "a large-scale game and language dataset for chess." How large is it?**

A6: Thank you for your comment. We have included a specific dataset statistics breakdown (including size, document count) in Table 9 of Appendix D.1.

**Q7: In line 42, it is mentioned, "from online chess databases." Could you please specify which databases are included in this reference?**

A7: The specific data background and sources for online chess databases are fully discussed in section 3.1.

**Q8: ... My question is, what is the contribution of this work? Is it about the dataset itself, training a Chat model, or does the dataset facilitate research in a specific aspect of LLMs? …  Furthermore, the author did not promote any specific field from the perspective of datasets or benchmarks, which does not align with the primary purpose of benchmarks.**

A8: Thank you for your comment. This work focuses on presenting a full pipeline to facilitate research into studying the interplay of natural language and decision-making (also refer to the motivation illustrated in global response). We believe what you mention (dataset, model and evaluation) is indeed an accurate summary of our contributions. 
We would like to know more about your understanding of contribution for dataset and benchmark and hope we can have more discussions about it.

**Q9: From my perspective, collecting data and training a model are relatively easy and straightforward tasks.**

A9: We politely disagree with the reviewer that the data collection and training are easy and straightforward. It's our belief that the entire process, from dataset curation to model training and evaluation, forms the foundation of Machine Learning/Deep Learning. We find it confusing that terms such as 'not challenging', 'easy', and 'straightforward' are used to describe these foundational aspects.  Furthermore, our dataset curation and training processes are anything but trivial. For instance, curating our dataset involved integrating numerous heterogeneous sources, which necessitated careful and thoughtful design along with extensive engineering efforts for collection, pre-processing, and cleaning.

Dear reviewers,

Thank you very much for your constructive reviews and precious comments in helping us improve the paper. We are writing to address your feedback and provide a detailed explanation of the changes made based on your comments. We have prepared a revision of our transcripts in accordance with these comments. In particular, we have made the following changes (all modified contents in our main paper and appendix are highlighted in red):

1. We updated our related work to include more recent references using LLM as agent, and also added several missing references.
2. We introduced a new figure, Figure 1, which serves as the cornerstone illustration of our paper, effectively showcasing the comprehensive pipeline of our study.
3. For readers unfamiliar with chess, we added Appendix B to explain various chess notation formats.
We added a new section, Appendix D, to present dataset statistics, examples, and quality metrics, helping readers better understand our dataset.
4. We included task plots and task examples in Appendix G to clarify the evaluation tasks.
5. We updated our qualitative results with the human error analysis found in Appendix H.
6. In Appendix I and figure 6, we presented the new ChessCLIP visualization demo to showcase its capabilities. Concurrently, an updated demo notebook has been made available on https://github.com/waterhorse1/ChessGPT/blob/main/chessclip_demo.ipynb.

We also would like to address the motivation of our paper as there are several common questions regarding it.

There has been growing interest in utilizing LLM for decision-making. For example GATO [1]. In many cases, high capacity LLMs are used for their strong modeling capability, but we think it wasn’t clear how knowledge embedded in the corpus can influence and improve an agent’s decision-making process.

In this work, we are interested in using chess as a proxy to study how natural language as a knowledge base can influence and improve AI’s decision making capability.
Chess is advantageous for this problem because there is ample amount of data on chess thanks to its popularity. both behavior data, as well as knowledge databases, are widely available.
Chess provides a domain in which both knowledge and behavior can be encoded in the same modality so it allows us to understand the interplay of language and behavior in a single modality.
Chess is very accessible. There is a large body of existing work and tools that can facilitate understanding a LLM that can perform chess-related tasks.

As such, we advocate using chess as a platform for studying how LLMs can take advantage of both Internet-scale knowledge base and behavior data to improve their capabilities NLP tasks as well as decision-making.
[1] Reed et, al., A Generalist Agent, TMLR, https://openreview.net/forum?id=1ikK0kHjvj

1. From my perspective, I didn't quite grasp the motivation behind the author's pursuit of this work. Could the author elaborate on it in detail? Additionally, a significant portion of the paper is dedicated to the background and the source of the Chess data, which, in my opinion, could be included in an appendix. Instead, the main body should focus on elucidating the significance, importance, and other core insights derived from the Chess data.

2. The author's literature review appears to be lacking, as the references cited seem insufficient and inaccurate. In line 22, the author references three papers in the context of models leveraging Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). I have no doubts about [20], "Constrained Value-Aligned LLM via Safe RLHF," as it is closely related to RLHF. However, the relevance of the other two papers, [43], "Tianxiang Sun and Xipeng Qiu. Moss, March 2023," and [43], "ChatGLM-6B, March 2023," to RLHF is not apparent to me.

How does the author perceive the significance of the following two papers in the context of RLHF?

- Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences
- Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

The entire paper appears to be roughly drafted, and there is considerable confusion in the references and literature review.

3. After reading the entire paper, it seems that the author summarized relevant online chess data to train ChessGPT, a 2.8B parameter pre-trained language model (mentioned in the hugging face dataset description as Model Description: A 2.8B parameter pre-trained language model in Chess.). However, in the main body of the paper, at line 248, the model is referred to as a 3B model. What could be the reason for this inconsistency?

Furthermore, I have the following two questions, and I kindly request the author to provide answers:

- In line 41, it is mentioned, "a large-scale game and language dataset for chess." How large is it?

- In line 42, it is mentioned, "from online chess databases." Could you please specify which databases are included in this reference?

In summary, the author collected online chess datasets (which is not a challenging task) and then trained ChessGPT and other models based on a 2.8B/3B parameter model. My question is, what is the contribution of this work? Is it about the dataset itself, training a Chat model, or does the dataset facilitate research in a specific aspect of LLMs? Does it enhance the essential capabilities of LLMs in any particular way? From my perspective, collecting data and training a model are relatively easy and straightforward tasks. Furthermore, the author did not promote any specific field from the perspective of datasets or benchmarks, which does not align with the primary purpose of benchmarks.

summary_and_contributions.value:
This paper creates a large-scale game and language dataset for chess and proposes novel models that integrate policy learning and language modeling in the context of Chess games. Traditionally, decision-making systems have either relied on historical policy data (gameplay data) or analytical insights presented in natural language. The authors argue that an efficient autonomous agent should leverage both sources of information.

To achieve this, they construct a large-scale dataset composed of Chess gameplay data and Chess-related language data (e.g., game analysis, books, online tutorials, etc.). Two models, ChessCLIP and ChessGPT, are introduced that utilize this hybrid dataset to learn.

ChessCLIP and ChessGPT are then evaluated based on their modeling ability (tracking game state), value judgment ability (assessing value and understanding Chess knowledge), and policy ability (decision-making). Experimental results demonstrate that these models outperform other large language model baselines across all evaluation tasks.

strengths.value: The release of ChessGPT and ChessCLIP, along with the large-scale dataset and the source code, represents valuable resources for the wider AI research community. The dataset is an extensive multimodal dataset of chess games and language descriptions of chess strategy and commentary that will be very useful for training multimodal chess models like theirs. Additionally, their trained models immediately can become useful for AI chess instruction and coaching. This paper is also a strong proof-of-concept for integrating policy learning and language modeling in general and beyond chess.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
* The paper could strengthen its contribution by including a comparison of ChessGPT and ChessCLIP to state-of-the-art (SOTA) chess models in the appendix. This would provide a better context for evaluating the effectiveness of the proposed models and approach. At the moment it is hard to put these models ability in perspective. It is unlikely these models outperform powerful methods like AlphaZero but it would be helpful to evaluate how close you can get to these other methods with this language model approach.
* Relatedly, it is unsurprising that these models outperform general LLMs that are not fine tuned for this task. In fact, these baseline LLMs do relatively poorly on most of these evaluations. Since there isn't a clear previous finetuned LLM baseline to compare against that I know of, it may be more fruitful for the authors to evaluate what the most valuable information sources in their dataset are for valuation performance. 
* As a non-chess expert, it was hard for me to completely understand the detail of their evaluations. Some visualizations might be helpful here.

limitations.value: The models, as currently presented, do not appear to have the ability to learn from their own gameplay experiences in contrast to RL algorithms, which is a limitation for the further enhancement of their policies. While this limitation could potentially be addressed in future work, the current models might not fully capture the dynamic nature of decision-making processes in the context of games.

relation_to_prior_work.value: They could elaborate more on the current state of chess playing AI

summary_and_contributions.value: In this paper, the authors introduced a large-scale game and language dataset for chess, and trained a models ChessCLIP and ChessGPT to tackle various chess-related tasks, and an evaluation benchmark for evaluating LLM's chess abilities. The dataset included millions of chess games stored in text format (including regular games, expert games, chess puzzles, etc), natural language datasets related to text, mixed game-language datasets (such as annotated chess games), and an instruction-tuning and conversation dataset about chess knowledge. Using these datasets, the authors first trained ChessCLIP (CLIP training between game states and text descriptions of game states) as a method to represent chess states, and  Chess-GPT, a GPT-3 based model that is finetuned on chess-related data. The models are then evaluated on a benchmark containing various tasks to determine the models' chess modeling abilities (finding all legal moves for a piece, board state tracking, etc) and value judgement abilities (determine which side has advantage, chess annotation multiple-choice, etc). The trained language model ChessGPT significant outperformed baselines such as LLAMA, thus demonstrating that the collected chess-related datasets really helps improve the language model's abilities in chess-related tasks.

strengths.value:
1. Teaching language models to reason about chess is a very challenging task. It is also significant for the research community, as it is known that large language models are not great at deducing complex tasks that involves many different moving objects and long sequences of moves (such as chess).
2. The collected dataset is very large in size (millions of games), and the data source comes from multiple different sources, thus making the data more diverse. This dataset can be very useful for researchers who want to explore the planning or long-term state tracking abilities of large language models.
3. The authors managed to train a GPT-3 type model that achieves significantly better performance on chess-related tasks compared to baseline large language models such as LLAMA.
4. The authors presented a new set of tasks for thoroughly evaluating a language model's ability in chess-related tasks, which will be very useful for future research to directly compare results in a standardized way.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: The presentation can improve a little bit. There doesn't seem to be enough visuals or examples illustrating each tasks. I am able to understand all tasks because I played quite a bit of online chess, but this may not be the case for all readers.

limitations.value: They were adequately addressed in section G of Appendix.

correctness.value: The dataset is constructed in a sound way, and the benchmark evaluation methods are reasonable and seems to be performed correctly.

clarity.value: Overall the writing is quite clear, although a bit more illustrations, examples and visuals on the tasks/outputs would help.

relation_to_prior_work.value: It is clear that this work differs from previous contributions.

documentation.value: The documentation is sufficient and comprehensive in the Appendix.

title.value: ChessGPT: Bridging Policy Learning and Language Modeling

abstract.value: When solving decision-making tasks, humans typically depend on information from two key sources: (1) Historical policy data, which provides interaction replay from the environment, and (2) Analytical insights in natural language form, exposing the invaluable thought process or strategic considerations. Despite this, the majority of preceding research focuses on only one source: they either use historical replay exclusively to directly learn policy or value functions, or engaged in language model training utilizing mere language corpus. In this paper, we argue that a powerful autonomous agent should cover both sources. Thus, we propose ChessGPT, a GPT model bridging policy learning and language modeling by integrating data from these two sources in Chess games. Specifically, we build a large-scale game and language dataset related to chess. Leveraging the dataset, we showcase two model examples ChessCLIP and ChessGPT, integrating policy learning and language modeling. Finally, we propose a full evaluation framework for evaluating language model's chess ability. Experimental results validate our model and dataset's effectiveness. We open source our code, model, and dataset at https://github.com/waterhorse1/ChessGPT.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')

supplementary_material.description: Supplementary material. All supplementary material must be self-contained and submitted as a PDF or multiple files zipped into a single file. Access to datasets and benchmarks may be provided via the URL field below.

URL.description: Public URL link to dataset or benchmark (if applicable). Instructions on how to access may also be provided here. open_credentialized_access.description: In exceptional cases, e.g. for ethical reasons, datasets can be released under an established open credentialized access procedure, (e.g. PhysioNet credentialing for use of human subject data). If this is a case, briefly describe here how to access the data. This field is publicly visible, hence not meant for sending a private access link to reviewers, you can do that after the initial submission by sending an official note to the reviewers. Please see the Call For Papers for more details. If unsure, leave this field open.
